nameStory: Siberian water-milfoil gets its name from its native range, which includes Siberia and other parts of northern Asia. The 'water-milfoil' part comes from its feathery underwater leaves that were thought to resemble the delicate, finely-divided leaves of milfoil herbs that grew on land.
description: Siberian water-milfoil is an aquatic plant that lives completely underwater except when it flowers. It grows as long, trailing green stems that can reach over three feet in length, creating underwater meadows in ponds and streams. The plant is covered with whorls of feathery, fan-like leaves that give it a soft, delicate appearance as it sways in the current.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, fan-like leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem, divided into many thread-like segments that feel soft and flexible when touched underwater

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long trailing stems that grow completely submerged, often forming dense underwater carpets that wave gently in the current

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green when alive and growing, but distinctive white color when dried or dead, feeling smooth and somewhat brittle

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers emerge above water surface on short spikes, appearing in summer as the only part of the plant you'll see above water

habitat: Look for Siberian water-milfoil in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow streams, and shallow lake edges throughout New England. It prefers areas with soft, muddy bottoms where it can root easily, and is often found in water 1-6 feet deep where sunlight can still reach the submerged leaves.

seasonality.spring: New green growth begins underwater as water temperatures warm, with fresh feathery leaves emerging from overwintering root systems.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush underwater foliage and small flower spikes poking above the water surface, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back and stems start turning from green to white, though some green growth may persist in warmer waters.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground growth dies back, leaving whitened stem fragments and dormant root systems that will regrow in spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'Siberian,' this water-milfoil is actually native to much of North America and isn't the aggressive invader that its cousin, Eurasian water-milfoil, has become - it's one of the 'good guys' in the milfoil family!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil, but Siberian water-milfoil has shorter, less dense flower spikes and tends to be less aggressive in its growth. Memory trick: Siberian is the 'shy' one with shorter spikes, while Eurasian is the 'aggressive' invader with longer, denser flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: The milfoil family can be confusing because there are many similar-looking species, some native and beneficial, others invasive and problematic. Learning to distinguish between them is important for lake and pond management, as some milfoils need protection while others need control.
compareHints: Siberian water-milfoil differs from other milfoils by its relatively short flower spikes and less aggressive spreading habit compared to invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil. Unlike some of its relatives, it tends to form smaller, less dense colonies and has flower spikes that barely emerge above the water surface, rather than the tall, prominent spikes of problem species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eurasian water-milfoil has more finely divided leaves than most of its native relatives, with leaflets that are thread-like and numerous.
Among New England's water-milfoils, broadleaf water-milfoil stands out for having distinctly broader surface leaves compared to most relatives like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Low water-milfoil is the shortest member of its genus in New England, staying under a foot tall while Eurasian water-milfoil can reach 10 feet long.
Unlike its native milfoil cousins that stay mostly submerged, parrot's feather boldly emerges above water with bright green foliage.
Among New England's water-milfoils, Slender Water-milfoil lives up to its name with the most delicate, thread-like leaf divisions.
Unlike the aggressive Eurasian water-milfoil which forms dense mats, alternate water-milfoil grows in looser colonies and has its distinctive alternately-arranged flowers rather than whorled ones.
Unlike the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil which has leaves scattered along the stem, whorled water-milfoil has its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement.
